title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
directAnswer: This is level-order traversal with one extra step. Run BFS, but process the queue one full level at a time: snapshot the queue's size before the inner loop, sum exactly that many nodes' values, divide by the count, and append the average. The size-snapshot is the trick that draws a clean boundary between levels. Use a long (or double) accumulator — node values can be near the int limit and a level of them overflows int.

remember.pattern: Level-by-level BFS with a per-level sum and count
remember.formula:
queue = [root]
while queue not empty:
    size = len(queue)            # freeze this level's width
    levelSum = 0
    for i in range(size):        # exactly one level
        node = queue.pop_front()
        levelSum += node.val
        enqueue node's children
    result.append(levelSum / size)
rules: Snapshot `size = queue.length` **before** the inner loop — it freezes the current level's width as children get enqueued.
Iterate exactly `size` times so the next level's nodes don't bleed into this level's sum.
Accumulate into a **long** (Java) or float (Python) — a level of int values can overflow a 32-bit int.
Divide by the **node count** of that level, not by anything fixed — levels have different widths.
Enqueue **non-null** children only; never push nulls or you'll divide by an inflated count.
whenToUse: You need a per-level aggregate (average, sum, max, min, count)
Processing must respect level boundaries — node depth matters
Breadth-first order is natural; you want results top-to-bottom by level
Any 'for each row of the tree, compute X' phrasing
antiSignals: Order within a level must alternate → still BFS, but Zigzag Level Order
You only need the last value of each level → Right Side View (take the last per level)
The aggregate is over root-to-leaf paths, not levels → DFS instead
Depth doesn't matter, just a global aggregate → a plain DFS sum is simpler
remember.takeaway: Average of Levels is the cleanest demonstration of the 'freeze the queue size' BFS template. Once you internalize snapshotting size before the inner loop, the entire family of level-order problems — sums, maxima, right-side view, zigzag — becomes the same loop with a different per-level reduction.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can run a level-aware BFS by snapshotting the queue size to delimit levels, and whether you anticipate integer overflow when summing many large values per level.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reading queue.size() inside the loop (so it changes as children are added, mixing levels), or summing into an int and overflowing on a wide level of near-max values.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the size-snapshot idiom explicitly, mention the overflow guard (long/double accumulator) before being asked, and note the DFS alternative that carries depth and tallies (sum, count) per level.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the **average value of the nodes on each level** in the form of an array.

Answers within `10⁻⁵` of the actual answer will be accepted.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10⁴]
The answer is an array of doubles, one per level, top to bottom
understanding: We must compute one number — the mean of all node values — for each level of the tree, and return them ordered from the root's level downward. The defining challenge is grouping nodes by depth, which BFS does naturally if we process the queue one level at a time. The value range reaching ±2³¹ is a deliberate hint that summing a level can overflow a 32-bit integer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can node values get, and does that affect the sum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: They span the full 32-bit range (±2³¹). A single level of many near-max values overflows int, so the running sum must be a long (or a double).

clarifyingQuestions.question: What order should the averages appear in?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Top to bottom — the root's level first, then each successive level. BFS produces exactly this order.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraint says at least 1 node, but a robust solution returns an empty list for a null root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: BFS or DFS?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: BFS is the natural fit because levels are the unit of work. DFS works too if you carry the depth and accumulate (sum, count) per level into parallel arrays.

examples.explanation: Same averages: level 1 is [9,20] and level 2 is [15,7].
A single Integer.MAX_VALUE node — its own average. Two such on one level would overflow an int sum, motivating a long accumulator.

approaches.name: Level-Order BFS with a Frozen Queue Size (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the natural and expected answer. Frame it as 'BFS, but reduce one level at a time by snapshotting the queue size'.
hints: Averages are per LEVEL, and BFS visits nodes level by level. How do you know where one level ends and the next begins inside the queue?
At the top of each outer iteration, the queue holds exactly one full level. Record its size first, then loop that many times, summing values and enqueuing children.
Divide the level's sum by the count you recorded. Watch the accumulator type — many large values can overflow a 32-bit int, so sum into a long or double.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once with O(1) work → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one level at a time, so its peak size is the maximum level width w → O(w) space, which is O(n) for a wide bottom level.
approaches.explanation:
Breadth-first traversal already visits nodes level by level; the only addition this problem needs is a way to know exactly where each level ends so we can reduce it independently. The elegant solution is to **snapshot the queue's size at the start of each outer iteration**.

**Why the size snapshot delimits levels.** At the moment we enter the outer `while`, the queue contains precisely the nodes of the current level and nothing else — we haven't enqueued any of their children yet. So `size = queue.length` captures that level's width. We then loop exactly `size` times, and during those iterations we *append* children to the back of the queue. Because we only iterate `size` times, those freshly-added children are untouched this round — they form the *next* level, to be processed on the following outer iteration. If instead we read `queue.length` live inside the loop, it would grow as children are added and we'd merge multiple levels into one sum.

**Why the accumulator must be wider than int.** The constraint allows node values up to `2³¹ − 1` (`Integer.MAX_VALUE`). A level can contain many such values, and even two of them sum to more than a 32-bit signed int can hold, wrapping around to a negative number. So in Java we accumulate into a `long` (or a `double`); in Python integers are arbitrary precision so the sum is safe, but we still divide as a float. This overflow guard is exactly the kind of detail interviewers probe — stating it unprompted signals real care.

**Why we divide by the recorded count, not a constant.** Levels widen as you descend (until the last, possibly-partial level), so each level has its own node count. We divide that level's sum by the `size` we snapshotted, producing the mean. Storing the count up front, before the queue mutates, keeps the division correct.

**Why only non-null children get enqueued.** We push a child only if it exists. Enqueuing nulls would inflate the next level's `size`, throwing off both the iteration count and the divisor, and would crash when we later read `.val` off a null. Skipping nulls keeps `size` equal to the true number of real nodes on the level.
approaches.insight: The whole template is 'freeze the width, then drain exactly that many'. That single line — `size = queue.length` before the inner loop — converts a flat BFS into a level-aware one, and it's the shared backbone of Level Order Traversal, Right Side View, Zigzag, and this problem. Change only the per-level reduction (here: sum then divide).

approaches.name: DFS Carrying Depth with Per-Level (sum, count)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as an alternative when asked for a recursive solution, or to show you can group by level without a queue.
hints: Without a queue, how do you know which level a node belongs to during a DFS? Pass the depth down.
Maintain two parallel arrays indexed by depth: one accumulating the sum of values at that depth, one counting nodes at that depth.
After the traversal, divide each level's sum by its count to get the averages, already in top-to-bottom order.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited once and updates its depth's tallies in O(1) → O(n) time. Recursion depth is the tree height h → O(h) stack space, plus O(L) for the per-level arrays where L is the number of levels (≤ n).
approaches.explanation:
BFS makes levels explicit through the queue, but DFS can group by level too if we carry the current depth as a parameter and tally into arrays indexed by depth.

**Why pass the depth.** In DFS we descend along paths rather than rows, so a node's level isn't implicit in the traversal order. Threading `depth` through each recursive call tells every node which bucket it belongs to. The root is depth 0, its children depth 1, and so on.

**Why two parallel arrays.** To compute an average we need both the total and the count for each level. `sums[d]` accumulates the values at depth `d`, and `counts[d]` accumulates how many nodes contributed. When we visit a node at depth `d`, we add its value to `sums[d]` and increment `counts[d]`. If `d` is a depth we've never reached, we extend the arrays first. As with BFS, the sum bucket should be a `long`/`double` to avoid overflow.

**Why the result comes out ordered.** Because depth `d` indexes directly into the arrays, level 0's tallies live at index 0, level 1's at index 1, and so on. After the DFS completes we walk the arrays from index 0 upward, dividing `sums[d] / counts[d]`, and the averages emerge already in top-to-bottom order — no sorting needed.

**Why this trades space differently than BFS.** DFS uses `O(h)` recursion stack instead of `O(w)` queue width, which can be a win on wide, shallow trees and a loss on deep, skinny ones. The per-level arrays add `O(L)` where `L` is the number of levels. Functionally identical result; the choice between BFS and DFS here is really a choice about which dimension (width vs height) you'd rather pay for.
approaches.insight: Indexing tallies by depth turns DFS into a level-grouping tool. Recognizing that 'a quantity per level' can be computed by either freezing the BFS queue or by depth-indexed accumulation in DFS is a transferable insight — pick whichever traversal's space profile suits the tree shape.

dryRun.intro: DFS carries depth; sums[d] and counts[d] accumulate per level. Divide at the end.

code.python:
def averageOfLevels(self, root: TreeNode) -> list[float]:
    sums: list[int] = []
    counts: list[int] = []

    def dfs(node: TreeNode, depth: int) -> None:
        if node is None:
            return
        if depth == len(sums):              # first node seen at this depth
            sums.append(0)
            counts.append(0)
        sums[depth] += node.val
        counts[depth] += 1
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)

    dfs(root, 0)
    return [sums[d] / counts[d] for d in range(len(sums))]

java.explanation: Start at depth 0; sums/counts grow as new depths are reached.
First time we reach this depth — extend both arrays with a fresh (0, 0) bucket.
Accumulate the value into this level's long sum, avoiding int overflow.
Descend with depth+1 so children land in the next level's bucket.

python.explanation: New depth reached — append a zero sum and zero count bucket.
Add to the level's total; Python ints can't overflow.
Track how many nodes contributed to this level's sum.

python.line: return [sums[d] / counts[d] for d in range(len(sums))]
python.explanation: Divide each level's total by its count; arrays are already in level order.

edgeCases.behavior: DFS recursion depth O(n); each level has one node so averages equal the spine values.
Long sum handles cancellation correctly; average can be negative.

pitfalls: Using int for the per-level sum array, reintroducing overflow.
Forgetting to extend the arrays when a new depth is first reached.
Passing the same depth to both children instead of depth+1.
Dividing with integer division instead of producing a float.

commonMistakes: Reading the queue size inside the loop instead of snapshotting it, merging adjacent levels.
Summing level values into a 32-bit int and overflowing on large inputs.
Enqueuing null children, inflating the level count and crashing on value access.
Performing integer division and losing the fractional part of the average.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Live queue size inside the loop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the inner loop bound re-reads queue.size() each iteration, it grows as children are enqueued, so you keep dequeuing into the same 'level' and merge multiple levels into one average.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on the level sum
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Node values reach Integer.MAX_VALUE. Summing several into an int wraps around to a negative number, producing a wildly wrong average.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer division of the average
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Dividing two ints in Java truncates toward zero, so 29/2 becomes 14 instead of 14.5. Cast the numerator (or use a double) before dividing.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: result.add((double) (sum / size));   // division happens in int first → 14.0
commonMistakesDetailed.good: result.add((double) sum / size);     // cast first → true 14.5

patternNote: Level-aware BFS via the frozen-queue-size idiom. Recognise it whenever you need a per-level aggregate or per-level grouping. Swap the reduction (sum/average, max, last element, full list) and the same loop solves Level Order Traversal, Right Side View, Largest Value in Each Row, and Zigzag.
